title: CBSE Class 10 English Language and Literature · Practice paper 2
subject: English Language and Literature
label: Practice paper
instr: This question paper contains 24 questions. All questions are compulsory.

The question paper is divided into three sections:
Section A: Reading Skills (20 marks), questions 1 and 2
Section B: Grammar and Creative Writing Skills (20 marks), questions 3 to 14
Section C: Literature (40 marks), questions 15 to 24

The board paper has 11 questions. Here they are numbered so that each task can be answered and marked on its own: questions 3 to 12 are the grammar tasks of board question 3; question 13 is the letter (board question 4); question 14 is the analytical paragraph (board question 5); questions 15 and 16 are the extract-based questions (board questions 6 and 7); questions 17 to 20 are from First Flight (board question 8); questions 21 and 22 are from Footprints without Feet (board question 9); questions 23 and 24 are the long answer questions (board questions 10 and 11).
Answer the short answer questions (17 to 22) in about 40-50 words each, and the letter, the analytical paragraph and the long answer questions (23 and 24) in about 100-120 words each.

Internal choices of the board paper are not included: each question has one version. Where the board paper lets you attempt ten of twelve grammar tasks or four of five short questions, this paper gives only the number you must answer.
Survey figures, names and places in the reading passages and the writing tasks are imaginary and created for practice.
This is a practice paper written in the pattern of the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. It is not an official CBSE paper.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following passage.

(1) A generation ago, when a radio stopped working or a shoe lost its sole, the first thought in most Indian homes was, "Who can fix this?" Every neighbourhood had its cobbler, its tailor and its electrician who could bring tired objects back to life. Today the first thought is more often, "Where can I buy a new one?" Repair has quietly given way to replacement, and we are poorer for it in more ways than one.

(2) Part of the reason is cost. Many electronic goods are now so cheap that a new one costs little more than mending the old one. Some products are deliberately designed so that their parts cannot be opened or replaced. Batteries are glued in, screws are hidden and spare parts are hard to find. Advertisements, too, keep telling us that the latest model is always better. When fixing something becomes difficult, throwing it away begins to feel natural.

(3) But the price tag in the shop is not the true cost. Every discarded phone, fan or mixer adds to a growing mountain of electronic waste, much of which contains harmful metals that can seep into soil and water. Making a replacement uses fresh raw materials and energy. A repaired object, on the other hand, carries on doing its job without any of these extra demands on the planet.

(4) There is also a human side to repair. A skilled repair person is a problem-solver who listens to a machine the way a doctor listens to a patient. When repair shops close, these skills disappear, and so do small livelihoods that have supported families for generations. Learning even simple repairs, such as stitching on a button or changing a fuse, also gives young people confidence. They begin to see objects not as mysterious boxes but as things they can understand.

(5) Around the world, people are pushing back. Volunteer-run "repair cafes" invite people to bring broken items and fix them together over a cup of tea. Some governments have begun to discuss a "right to repair", which would require companies to make spare parts and repair manuals available. Some schools now run workshops where students take apart old gadgets to see how they work.

(6) None of this means we should never buy anything new. It means pausing before we throw something away and asking whether it deserves a second life. Repair may cost a little time and effort, but the reward is worth it. A world that repairs is a world that wastes less, values skill and respects the things it owns.

parts.q: (i) What does the writer mean by saying that repair has 'quietly given way to replacement'? (Paragraph 1)
parts.model: Slowly, and without people noticing much, the habit of fixing things has been replaced by the habit of buying new ones.

points.t: The habit of repairing has slowly/unnoticed been replaced by the habit of buying new things

parts.q:
(ii) Complete the following with the correct option from the two given.
When the writer says, 'the price tag in the shop is not the true cost' (paragraph 3), the writer refers to ________.
(a) the hidden harm to the environment caused by throwing away and replacing things
(b) the extra money shopkeepers charge for delivery and installation
parts.model: (a) the hidden harm to the environment caused by throwing away and replacing things. [The paragraph goes on to describe electronic waste, harmful metals, raw materials and energy.]

points.t: Option (a)

parts.q:
(iii) Which of the following is an example of a product 'deliberately designed' to be hard to repair, as described in paragraph 2?
A. A bicycle whose chain can be replaced at any local shop
B. A phone whose battery is glued in so that it cannot be removed
C. A table fan sold with a free repair manual
D. A wooden chair held together with ordinary screws
parts.model: B. A phone whose battery is glued in so that it cannot be removed.

points.t: Option B

parts.q: (iv) In paragraph 4, the writer compares a repair person to a doctor. What does this comparison show about repair work?
parts.model: The writer says a skilled repair person listens to a machine the way a doctor listens to a patient, that is, finds out what is wrong before treating it. This shows that repair is skilled problem-solving that needs knowledge and care, not a simple manual job, and so it deserves respect.

points.t: The comparison: a repair person listens to/diagnoses a machine as a doctor does a patient
It shows repair is skilled, careful problem-solving that deserves respect

parts.q:
(v) State whether the following statement is True or False. (Paragraph 4)
Learning simple repairs makes young people see objects as mysterious boxes.
parts.model: False. [Learning repairs makes them see objects 'not as mysterious boxes but as things they can understand'.]

points.t: False

parts.q:
(vi) Complete the analogy by selecting the correct option, (a) or (b).
repair cafe : fixing broken items together :: right to repair : ________
(a) making spare parts and repair manuals available
(b) buying new gadgets at lower prices
parts.model: (a) making spare parts and repair manuals available. [Each idea is paired with what it involves, as described in paragraph 5.]

points.t: Option (a)

parts.q:
(vii) Read the statements (i)-(v) and select the option that correctly classifies them as Facts (F) or Opinions (O).
(i) Much electronic waste contains harmful metals.
(ii) We are poorer because repair has given way to replacement.
(iii) Volunteer-run repair cafes invite people to bring broken items.
(iv) A world that repairs respects the things it owns.
(v) Some products have their batteries glued in.
A. (i) O (ii) O (iii) F (iv) F (v) F
B. (i) F (ii) O (iii) F (iv) O (v) F
C. (i) F (ii) F (iii) O (iv) O (v) F
D. (i) F (ii) O (iii) O (iv) O (v) F
parts.model: B. (i) F (ii) O (iii) F (iv) O (v) F

points.t: Option B

parts.q: (viii) Why does the writer begin the passage by recalling how things were 'a generation ago'?
parts.model: Recalling the past sets up a contrast between a time when repairing was the natural first thought and today's habit of buying new things. It makes readers think back, perhaps with nostalgia, and question their own habits, which prepares them for the writer's argument that something valuable has been lost.

points.t: Contrast between the past habit of repairing and today's habit of replacing
Engages readers (nostalgia, questioning their habits) and introduces the argument that something valuable has been lost

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following passage.

(1) Many Indian towns face water shortages in the summer months, and much of the pressure comes from the way water is used at home. To understand this better, a resident welfare group in Navpur, a mid-sized town, studied how much water an average person in 120 homes used each day and for what purposes.

(2) The study found that each person used about 135 litres of water a day. The table shows how this was divided.
ActivityLitres per person per day
Bathing45
Flushing toilets35
Washing clothes25
Cleaning utensils and floors18
Drinking and cooking7
Other uses (gardening, washing vehicles)5


(3) Only a small share of the water was used for drinking and cooking. Most of it went into bathing, flushing and washing, where much could be saved. The group noted that a bucket bath uses about 20 litres, while a long shower can use 60 litres or more. Old toilet cisterns used up to 12 litres per flush, compared with 6 litres or less for newer dual-flush models.

(4) The study also found leaking taps in nearly one-third of the homes. A tap that drips all day can waste several litres without anyone noticing. The group advised families to check their taps and pipes regularly.

(5) The group has now begun a campaign called "Every Drop Counts". It encourages families to fix leaks, use buckets instead of showers and reuse the water from washing vegetables to water their plants.

parts.q:
(i) Complete the sentence by selecting the correct option from those given in the bracket.
The phrase 'much of the pressure comes from the way water is used at home' (paragraph 1) suggests that household water use ________. (is a major cause of shortages / has no effect on shortages)
parts.model: is a major cause of shortages

points.t: is a major cause of shortages

parts.q: (ii) Why did the resident welfare group carry out the study? (Paragraph 1)
parts.model: To understand how water was used at home, that is, how much water an average person used each day, because the town faced water shortages in summer.

points.t: To find out how much water a person used at home each day (to understand the pressure behind summer shortages)

parts.q:
(iii) Select the option that is true for the assertion and reason given below.
Assertion: Bathing accounts for one-third of the water used by a person each day.
Reason: A bucket bath uses about 20 litres of water.
A. Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation.
B. Both are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation.
C. The assertion is true, but the reason is false.
D. The assertion is false, but the reason is true.
parts.model: B. Both are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation. [45 out of 135 litres is one-third, and a bucket bath does use about 20 litres, but this fact does not explain the share of bathing.]

points.t: Option B

parts.q:
(iv) Choose the correct option to complete the sentence.
All of the following can be concluded from the table EXCEPT ________.
A. Flushing toilets uses five times as much water as drinking and cooking.
B. Washing clothes and cleaning utensils and floors together use more water than bathing.
C. Drinking and cooking use about 5% of the total.
D. Bathing is the single largest use of water.
parts.model: B. Washing clothes and cleaning utensils and floors together use more water than bathing. [25 + 18 = 43 litres, which is less than 45. A: 35 = 5 x 7; C: 7 out of 135 is about 5%; D: 45 litres is the largest.]

points.t: Option B

parts.q: (v) Compare the water used by a bucket bath with that used by a long shower. What does this suggest about how families in Navpur could save water? (Paragraphs 2 and 3)
parts.model: A bucket bath uses about 20 litres, while a long shower can use 60 litres or more, which is three times as much. Since bathing is the largest single use (45 litres per person per day), families could save a great deal of water by taking bucket baths instead of long showers.

points.t: Correct comparison: about 20 litres against 60 litres or more (about three times as much)
Inference: switch to bucket baths; as bathing is the largest use, the saving would be large

parts.q:
(vi) Complete the sentence suitably. (Paragraph 3)
Replacing old toilet cisterns with dual-flush models saves water because ________.
parts.model: the new models use 6 litres or less per flush instead of up to 12 litres, so at least half the water is saved on each flush

points.t: New models use 6 litres or less per flush compared with up to 12 litres (half or more saved)

parts.q: (vii) Identify the phrase from paragraph 3 which shows that water use in some activities can be reduced.
parts.model: 'where much could be saved'

points.t: where much could be saved

parts.q: (viii) A family in Navpur washes vegetables every morning. Based on paragraph 5, suggest how they could make better use of this water.
parts.model: They could collect the water used for washing vegetables and reuse it to water their plants.

points.t: Collect the water and reuse it to water plants

parts.q: (ix) Suggest one reason why 'Every Drop Counts' is a suitable title for the passage.
parts.model: The passage shows how everyday uses and small leaks add up to a large amount of water, and it ends with a campaign of that name that urges families to save water.

points.t: Links the title to the content: small uses/leaks add up, and the passage ends with the campaign urging families to save water

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Select the correct option to complete the line from a school newsletter.
Our school ________ the inter-school quiz three times since 2020.
questions.sol: 'Since 2020' links a past period with the present, so the present perfect 'has won' is correct.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Report the librarian's request.
The librarian said to the students, "Please keep your phones on silent mode."
questions.model: The librarian requested the students to keep their phones on silent mode.

points.t: Correct reported form: The librarian requested/asked the students to keep their phones on silent mode

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank.
________ of my two brothers live in Pune.
questions.sol: 'Both' refers to two people together and takes a plural verb ('live'). 'Each' and 'either' would need 'lives'; 'every' cannot be followed by 'of'.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Identify the error in the given line from a school report and supply the correction.
Neither the principal nor the teachers was present at the meeting.
Use the format: Error | Correction

points.t: Error: was; Correction: were (with 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'teachers')

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Select the correct option to complete the advice.
You look tired. You ________ take a short break before you continue.
questions.sol: 'Should' gives advice and is followed by the base form. 'Ought' needs 'to', 'used to' describes a past habit, and 'has to' does not agree with 'you'.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Aman's mother asked him, "Have you finished your project?"
Report the question by completing the sentence.
Aman's mother asked him ________.
questions.model: Aman's mother asked him if/whether he had finished his project.

points.t: if/whether he had finished his project

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
The given sentence has an error. Select the option that correctly identifies the error and the correction.
Yesterday the electrician come late but fixed the fan in ten minutes.
questions.sol: 'Yesterday' needs the simple past, and the second verb 'fixed' is also past, so 'come' must be 'came'.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb given in the bracket.
Look! The children ________ (fly) kites on the terrace.

points.t: are flying

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Fill in the blank by choosing the correct option from those given in the bracket.
There is ________ milk left, so we can still make tea for two. (little / a little)

points.t: a little

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Select the option that correctly reports the doctor's advice.
The doctor said to the patient, "Do not skip your medicines."
options: The doctor advised the patient not to skip the medicines.
The doctor advised the patient to not skipped the medicines.
The doctor said the patient do not skip your medicines.
The doctor told the patient that don't skip the medicines.
questions.sol: A negative command is reported with 'not to' + base form after a reporting verb such as 'advised'.

questions.subject: English
questions.text: You are Ishaan Verma, Head Boy of Green Valley School, Dehradun. Every year, many good textbooks are thrown away or sold as waste paper when students move to the next class. Write a letter in about 120 words to the Principal, requesting permission to set up a book bank in the school where students can donate and borrow used textbooks. Explain how it will help students and the environment.
questions.model:
Green Valley School
Dehradun
8 April 2027

The Principal
Green Valley School
Dehradun

Subject: Request to set up a book bank

Respected Sir/Madam

I am writing on behalf of the Student Council to request your permission to set up a book bank in our school.

Every year, many students buy new textbooks while their seniors' books, still in good condition, are thrown away or sold as waste paper. A book bank would allow students who have passed a class to donate their books, which juniors could then borrow free of cost.

This would reduce the burden on families who find books expensive. It would also save paper and teach students to share and reuse.

The Student Council will manage the collection and keep records. We only need a small room and a cupboard.

I hope you will kindly consider our request.

Yours sincerely
Ishaan Verma
Head Boy

points.t: Format: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, complimentary close and name, all in the correct places
Content: the need is explained (good books wasted every year) and the idea of the book bank is stated (donate and borrow)
Content: benefits are given (saves families money, saves paper, encourages sharing) with a practical plan
Organisation: ideas in logical paragraphs (purpose, need, benefits, plan, closing request) joined with suitable linkers
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct and the tone is formal and polite

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the cues below about weekend cycling clubs, which are becoming popular in many Indian cities.
• improve fitness and mental well-being
• cost far less than a gym membership
• use no fuel and cause no pollution
• build friendships across age groups
• few dedicated cycle tracks
• safety risks in heavy traffic
• extreme heat and heavy rain in some months
Write an analytical paragraph in about 120 words analysing the reasons for the popularity of cycling clubs and the challenges they face.
questions.model: Weekend cycling clubs have become popular in Indian cities, and several reasons explain this trend. Firstly, cycling improves physical fitness and also refreshes the mind. Secondly, it costs far less than a gym membership, so many people can afford it. Moreover, since bicycles use no fuel and cause no pollution, many riders see cycling as a way to help the environment. The clubs also build friendships across age groups. However, the trend faces serious challenges. Most cities have few dedicated cycle tracks, so riders must share roads with heavy traffic, which is risky. In addition, extreme heat and heavy rain make cycling difficult in some months. Overall, cycling clubs offer clear benefits, but safer roads and tracks are needed if the trend is to grow.

points.t: Content: the reasons for popularity are analysed using the cues (fitness, low cost, no pollution, friendships)
Content: the challenges are analysed (few tracks, traffic risks, weather) and a balanced conclusion is drawn
Organisation: an introductory sentence and a concluding statement; no title
Organisation: points in a logical order, linked with words such as firstly, moreover, however, overall
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow.

The young seagull was alone on his ledge. His two brothers and his sister had already flown away the day before. He had been afraid to fly with them. Somehow when he had taken a little run forward to the brink of the ledge and attempted to flap his wings he became afraid. The great expanse of sea stretched down beneath, and it was such a long way down — miles down.
(His First Flight, Liam O'Flaherty)

parts.q:
(i) Complete the sentence suitably.
The young seagull is 'alone on his ledge' while his brothers and sister have flown away. This suggests that he felt ________.
parts.model: lonely and left behind

points.t: lonely / left behind / isolated

parts.q:
(ii) What stopped the young seagull from flying, according to the extract?
A. He was too weak because he had not eaten.
B. His parents had told him not to fly yet.
C. He became afraid when he saw the great expanse of sea below.
D. His wings had been hurt on the ledge.
parts.model: C. He became afraid when he saw the great expanse of sea below.

points.t: Option C

parts.q:
(iii) Fill in the blank with the correct option from the bracket.
The phrase 'miles down' is an example of ________ that shows how frightening the height seemed to the young seagull. (exaggeration / understatement)
parts.model: exaggeration

points.t: exaggeration

parts.q: (iv) How does this extract set up the change that the young seagull goes through by the end of the story?
parts.model: The extract shows the seagull as fearful and alone, unable to trust his own wings although his brothers and sister have flown. Later, hunger and the sight of his mother holding a fish make him dive at it, and he finds that he can fly. Because the story opens with his fear, his final success is more meaningful: he moves from fear and self-doubt to courage and confidence.

points.t: The extract shows his fear, self-doubt and loneliness
Contrast with the ending: hunger and his mother's fish make him dive and fly; he moves from fear to confidence

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow.

Some say the world will end in fire,
Some say in ice.
From what I've tasted of desire
I hold with those who favour fire.
(Fire and Ice, Robert Frost)

parts.q:
(i) Complete the sentence suitably.
In these lines, 'fire' stands for ________.
parts.model: desire (greed, passion)

points.t: desire / greed / passion

parts.q:
(ii) What does the phrase 'From what I've tasted of desire' suggest about the speaker?
A. He has never felt any strong wishes.
B. He knows from his own experience how powerful desire can be.
C. He believes that desire is always harmless.
D. He enjoys the taste of fire.
parts.model: B. He knows from his own experience how powerful desire can be.

points.t: Option B

parts.q:
(iii) Fill in the blank with ONE suitable word.
The repetition of 'Some say' at the start of the first two lines shows that people hold ________ views about how the world will end.
parts.model: different (also accept: differing, opposing, contrasting)

points.t: different / differing / opposing

parts.q: (iv) How does the poet use the familiar question of how the world will end to say something about human behaviour?
parts.model: Frost takes a common question about the end of the world and turns it into a comment on human emotions. Fire stands for desire and greed, which can grow without limit and consume everything. By siding with fire, the speaker suggests that uncontrolled human desire, rather than a natural disaster, could destroy the world. The poem is a warning to control our emotions.

points.t: Fire = desire/greed, an emotion that grows without limit and can consume everything
The end of the world becomes a warning that uncontrolled human emotions could destroy it

questions.subject: English
questions.text: What are the 'twin obligations' that Mandela speaks of, and why could he not fulfil both of them in South Africa? (Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom)
questions.model: Every man has an obligation to his family (parents, wife and children) and to his people, community and country. In a civil, humane society he can fulfil both. In South Africa, a man of colour who tried to serve his people was torn from his family and forced into a life of secrecy and rebellion, so Mandela could not fulfil his duties as a son, brother, father and husband.

points.t: Content: the twin obligations: to one's family, and to one's people, community and country
Content: in South Africa, serving his people tore a man of colour from his family (life apart, secrecy, rebellion), so he failed as son, brother, father and husband
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: Why did Anne Frank feel that she needed a diary, and why did she decide to call it 'Kitty'? (From the Diary of Anne Frank)
questions.model: Anne had loving parents, a sister and about thirty people she called friends, but with them she talked only about ordinary everyday things and could not confide in anyone. She had no true friend, and she felt that 'paper has more patience than people'. So she wanted the diary itself to be her friend, and to bring this long-awaited friend alive in her imagination, she named it 'Kitty'.

points.t: Content: she had family and many friends but could not confide in anyone; no true friend; 'paper has more patience than people'
Content: she wanted the diary to be her friend, not a record of facts, so she gave it a name, 'Kitty'
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: How is the ending of 'The Tale of Custard the Dragon' ironic? (The Tale of Custard the Dragon, Ogden Nash)
questions.model: When the pirate climbed in, Mustard fled, Ink hid, Blink ran into a mousehole and Belinda cried for help. Only Custard, the 'coward', attacked and gobbled up the pirate. Yet afterwards Mustard, Ink and Blink boast that they would have been braver, Custard agrees that everybody is braver than he is, and he still cries for a nice safe cage. The true hero is still thought a coward.

points.t: Content: in the crisis the 'brave' pets and Belinda flee or cry for help, while 'cowardly' Custard alone fights and eats the pirate
Content: afterwards the others boast, Custard agrees everyone is braver and still cries for a safe cage: the real hero is still called a coward
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: What does the old religious man's argument suggest about the nature of true love? (For Anne Gregory, W. B. Yeats)
questions.model: The young man says that no one will love Anne for herself alone because of her yellow hair, and Anne replies that she could dye it. The old religious man has found a text proving that only God could love her for herself alone. This suggests that human love is drawn by outer beauty, and love for inner qualities alone is rare, almost divine.

points.t: Content: the argument: only God can love Anne for herself alone and not her yellow hair
Content: the meaning: human love is drawn by outward beauty; pure love for inner qualities is rare/divine
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: Why did Hari Singh return to Anil after stealing his money? (The Thief's Story)
questions.model: After stealing the money, Hari went to the station but did not board the train. He realised that the reading and writing Anil was teaching him could make him a respected man who earned far more than a few hundred rupees. He also thought of Anil's trust. So he returned and put the money back under the mattress.

points.t: Content: education/learning to read and write would bring him more than the stolen money
Content: Anil's trust and kindness; he returned and put the money back under the mattress
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: How does Bholi's refusal to marry Bishamber show the change in her? (Bholi)
questions.model: Bholi had been a shy, stammering girl whom her family treated as a burden. Education and her teacher's encouragement gave her confidence. When Bishamber, an old lame man, demanded a dowry of five thousand rupees at the wedding, Bholi spoke out clearly and refused to marry such a greedy, mean man. She stood up for her own dignity.

points.t: Content: the earlier Bholi: shy, stammering, treated as a burden; school and the teacher gave her confidence
Content: at the wedding she refuses the greedy Bishamber, who demanded dowry, showing courage and self-respect
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: How does the Buddha help Kisa Gotami accept the death of her son, and why is his method more effective than simply telling her the truth? (The Sermon at Benares)
questions.model: Kisa Gotami lost her only son. In her grief she carried the dead child to all her neighbours, asking them for medicine, and people said she had lost her senses. The Buddha did not tell her directly that the dead cannot return. Instead, he asked her to bring a handful of mustard seed from a house where no one had lost a child, husband, parent or friend. She went from house to house, but every family had lost someone. Gradually she understood that death is common to all and that her grief had been selfish. Because she discovered this truth for herself, it went deeper than any words could have done. The Buddha's method led her from despair to wisdom and peace.

points.t: Content: her grief: she lost her only son and carried him to her neighbours asking for medicine
Content: the Buddha's task: mustard seed from a house where no one had lost a child, husband, parent or friend
Content: why it works: she discovers for herself that death is common to all, so the lesson is deeper and lasting
Expression: ideas are organised logically, with an opening and a conclusion
Expression: the answer is fluent, relevant and in about 100-120 words
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct

questions.subject: English
questions.text: Horace Danby, a careful thief, ends up in prison because of a young lady. Discuss how the title 'A Question of Trust' is ironic. (A Question of Trust)
questions.model: Horace Danby was a careful thief who planned the robbery at Shotover Grange in detail. But while he was at work, a young lady surprised him with a voice from the doorway. He trusted her without finding out who she really was, and she played on his fear of being sent to prison. Eager to please her and to be let off, he forgot his own careful methods: he even took off his gloves to give her his lighter. She was in fact a thief herself, and she robbed the safe without leaving a single fingerprint, while Horace ended up in prison. The irony is that a thief, who lives by deceiving others, was ruined because he trusted a stranger blindly. Trust, which a thief can least afford, became his downfall.

points.t: Content: Horace is a careful thief who plans the robbery at Shotover Grange; the young lady surprises him
Content: he trusts her blindly; fearing prison, he forgets his caution (takes off his gloves to give her his lighter); she robs the safe without leaving fingerprints and he goes to prison
Content: the irony: a deceiver is himself deceived; trusting a stranger becomes his downfall
Expression: ideas are organised logically, with an opening and a conclusion
Expression: the answer is fluent, relevant and in about 100-120 words
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct
